They stay in camp with their backs to the mountain
b.explanation: The way they face shows participation, while the stone line shows where they stop.

b.prompt: Where does Moses stand, and how does that position help him point out the mountain?
options: Behind the watchers, so they turn away from him
At the summit, so they see him through the cloud
In front of the watchers, so they can follow his hand
b.explanation: Moses’ position and his gesture lead the crowd’s gaze toward the mountain.

b.prompt: The Israelites walked between the waters at the sea. What here explains how their route at Sinai differs?
options: There is open ground, so everyone is about to climb the mountain
The people gather below a mountain set apart for the meeting
Moses stands with the people, so the meeting is already over
b.explanation: At the sea a path opens for the people, but at Sinai they attend the meeting from the foot of the mountain.

teen.prompt: Which combination marks a place one can look toward but not see into clearly?
options: Sunlight makes everything on the summit visible
Light draws attention to the summit while cloud conceals it
Open ground below hides the summit from viewers
teen.explanation: Light and concealment occupy the same point, fitting the encounter’s tension between disclosure and concealment.

teen.prompt: Which evidence presents the boundary as an instruction the people heed as well as a feature of the landscape?
options: The stones form a line and the crowd stops on one side
Both the stones and the mountain are made of rock
There are more stones near the watchers than at the summit
teen.explanation: A line alone could be scenery; the crowd’s position in relation to it gives it a function.

teen.prompt: How does Moses’ position make him both part of the people and a mediator between them and the mountain?
options: He is above the cloud and can see both camps
He faces the people and his back hides the mountain from them
He stands on their side but directs their gaze toward the mountain
teen.explanation: His position places him with the crowd, and his gesture links them to the distant focus.

teen.prompt: What distinguishes evidence that the people keep their distance from evidence of why they do so?
options: The distance is visible, but the fear and the instruction come from the account
The distance proves that everyone feels the same fear
Everyone facing the mountain must want to climb it
teen.explanation: The gap shows where people stand; an emotional response and an instruction also require reading the text.

c.prompt: How do the foreground stones and the cloud at the summit give form to two kinds of limit?
options: They mark two permissible routes of ascent
One suggests a limit on movement and the other on sight
One marks the place of speech and the other the horn’s volume
c.explanation: The stones divide the space while the cloud obscures the view even from below.

c.prompt: What belongs to the wording of the command to set bounds, and what belongs to the illustrator’s choice?
options: The boundary is prescribed; the line of stones is its pictorial realization
The text prescribes a line of stones; distance from the mountain is added by the artist
Both the number of stones and each spectator’s position are fixed by the command
c.explanation: The command sets a limit without specifying a row of stones like the one depicted.

c.prompt: How does Moses’ gesture connect the viewer’s position with the mediating role assigned to him?
options: The viewer stands at the summit and sees Moses only through the crowd’s eyes
The viewer’s eye passes from the people through Moses toward the mountain
Moses and the people turn away from the mountain, isolating it from view
c.explanation: The gesture establishes a visual link between the two spaces without reproducing speech.

c.prompt: Which aspect of the Sinai event can the illustration convey directly?
options: The exact words uttered at that moment
The volume each person heard
The crowd's distance and the cloud before its eyes
c.explanation: The crowd's position, Moses' hand and the cloud provide visual evidence.

a.prompt: If you were in the crowd, how could you tell which man Moses was introducing?
options: He stands the man beside him and gestures toward him
He faces the crowd with everyone behind him
He has everyone in the crowd stand beside him
a.explanation: The chosen man stands beside Moses where the crowd can see him.

a.prompt: Joshua was standing beside Moses before. What changes when Moses gives him the role?
options: Moses bows his head and Joshua lays a hand on him
Both turn and lay a hand on the priest
Joshua bows his head and Moses lays a hand on him
a.explanation: Moses’ hand on Joshua shows the people whom he is giving the role to.

a.prompt: Joshua kneels and everyone watches. Why do this where the people can see?
options: So only Joshua knows about the role
So the people know whom to follow
So each person can pick a different leader
a.explanation: When Moses gives Joshua the role in public, everyone knows the next leader.

a.prompt: A friend arrives after the ceremony. What can the people who stood around tell her?
options: We saw Joshua give Moses the job of leading
We saw the crowd give Joshua the role without Moses
We saw Moses show everyone that Joshua would lead after him
a.explanation: By laying a hand on Joshua in public, Moses shows the people who will lead after him.

b.prompt: Who presents and who is presented? What distinguishes them even before the laying on of hands?
options: The staff bearer gestures toward the man beside him before the crowd
The man beside Moses speaks alone while Moses withdraws
The crowd points out two candidates standing far away
b.explanation: The staff identifies Moses and his gesture directs attention to Joshua.

b.prompt: A friend says Joshua is giving Moses the role. Which pair of details shows it is the other way around?
options: Both are in the middle and the priest stands nearby
Moses extends his hands and Joshua bows his head
The crowd and Joshua are looking toward Moses
b.explanation: The hands reach from the one appointing to the head of the man being appointed.

b.prompt: What in the scene distinguishes a private blessing from the public choice of a leader?
options: The assembly surrounds Joshua and watches the act
Joshua kneels while Moses touches him
Moses and Joshua are close to each other
b.explanation: A private blessing could include touch too, but here the people witness the appointment.

b.prompt: If someone claims Joshua received his role in secret, which evidence would help test the claim?
options: Joshua is near Moses and can hear him
Moses draws near to Joshua carrying a staff
People stand facing Moses and see his hand on Joshua
b.explanation: The direction of the onlookers’ gaze and the position of the hand together show witnesses to the appointment.

teen.prompt: How can you distinguish presenting a candidate from his actually leading, and which does this image depict?
options: Joshua stands near Moses and is therefore already leading the journey alone
Moses gestures toward the man before the crowd; Joshua is not yet leading them
The people look at both men, so they have identical roles as leaders
teen.explanation: Presentation before the community is visible here; Joshua’s leadership belongs to what follows.

teen.prompt: What do this gesture and Moses’ petition on the people’s behalf share, and how do they differ?
options: Both ask the crowd to choose someone else instead of Joshua
Both provide for continuing leadership; the hand gives the petition public expression
The petition presents Joshua to witnesses, and the gesture is between Moses and God alone
teen.explanation: The petition opens the episode; the visible contact with Joshua puts the appointment into effect.

teen.prompt: What turns Joshua’s kneeling from an encounter between two people into an act that the whole assembly witnesses?
options: The onlookers’ gazes converge where Moses and Joshua meet
Joshua is lower than Moses at the moment of contact
Moses extends one or more hands toward Joshua’s head
teen.explanation: Posture and touch show the action; the gazes establish to whom it is made visible.

teen.prompt: How can the picture address the claim that the priest appoints Joshua in Moses’ place?
options: Infer that the one wearing distinctive clothes must also carry out the appointment
Infer that Moses merely watches because the assembly stands behind him too
Distinguish the priest’s presence from Moses’ hands on Joshua
teen.explanation: A recognizable witness can take part in the ceremony without being the one who lays on hands.

c.prompt: How do the pictured spectators and the command in Numbers 27 distinguish two readings of Joshua standing beside Moses?
options: A public presentation as a stage in appointment, beyond mere closeness between teacher and pupil
Proof of immediately equal authority because the two stand at the same height
Proof that the assembly chose Joshua because it stands before him
c.explanation: The command to present him before the assembly gives the onlookers a function not explained by personal closeness alone.

c.prompt: The breastpiece helps identify Eleazar. Which conclusion about his authority also requires the text?
options: That his dress distinguishes him from the surrounding people
That he will seek judgment by the Urim for Joshua
That he stands near Moses during the appointment
c.explanation: The garment identifies a priest; his role in consulting the Urim for Joshua is stated in Numbers 27:21.

c.prompt: How does the image arrange the sightlines of a public appointment, and what does that leave unproved?
options: Joshua sees only Moses, so the appointment is concealed from the community
The crowd surrounds them, so each member participates in laying on hands
The people can see Joshua and Moses; their unanimous consent is not depicted
c.explanation: “Before the whole assembly” describes visibility; witnessing is distinct from voting or performing the act.

c.prompt: Which distribution of roles fits both the hands visible here and the sequence of instructions in Numbers 27?
options: The assembly designates Joshua, the priest lays hands on him, and Moses watches
Moses alone chooses, the assembly lays hands, and the priest receives a later report
God designates Joshua, Moses lays hands on him, and the priest and assembly are present
c.explanation: The text establishes who gives the instruction, while gesture and witnesses show its execution.
